docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
Prebuilt libraries and required header files packaged in archives.

  • Latest stable build: v1.85.3
  • Last stable build requiring only C++11 support: v1.46.7
  • For several modern Visual Studio Compilers:
    • Visual Studio 2026 - MSVC 145 - from v1.85.0
    • Visual Studio 2022 - MSVC 143
    • Visual Studio 2019 - MSVC 142 - until v1.84.x
    • Visual Studio 2017 - MSVC 141 - until v1.45.1 (and v1.46.7)
    • Visual Studio 2015 - MSVC 140 - until v1.45.2
  • For both 32- and 64-Bit architectures
  • Convenient with all three build configurations Release, RelWithDebInfo, Debug

What is code without examples - harder to understand, less practical to get stated with, and so on.

  • Several easy starter examples from the official gRPC project
    • For Visual Studio 2022, Visual Studio 2019
    • Tested with gRPC versions v1.42.0 and above
    • Maintained at Cpp-gRPC-Visual-Studio-Examples
    • New examples taken directly from the gRPC repository are available on the v2-next-gen-2022 branch - please test and give feedback
    • For older versions of Visual Studio e.g. Visual Studio 2017 and Visual Studio 2015 until version 1.45.2
    • Pre-configured - Can be used in seconds.
    • Debuggable - RelWithDebInfo and Debug include symbols

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
One of the compilers:

  • Visual Studio 2026 - MSVC 145
  • Visual Studio 2022 - MSVC 143
  • Visual Studio 2019 - MSVC 142 (up to v1.84.x)

gRPC C++ v1.47.0 and later require C++14.

For a better experience use one of the IDEs with one the upper mentioned compilers.

docs.title: What is Cpp-gRPC-Windows-PreBuilts?
docs.text:
Cpp-gRPC-Windows-PreBuilts provides prebuilt gRPC C++ libraries for Windows and Visual Studio. You download ready-to-use ZIP archives, extract them, and link against gRPC without building it from source.

Each release contains:

  • Library archives (for example MSVC143_64.zip) with the headers and precompiled libraries for one compiler and one architecture.
  • Examples (Examples.zip) with preconfigured Visual Studio solutions for the official gRPC C++ examples.
  • Build information that records the compilers, SDKs and settings used for the build (tracked since v1.22.0).

The project is split across these repositories:

Repository Content Cpp-gRPC-Windows-PreBuilts Overview, release table and this documentation gRPC_windows Release downloads (ZIP archives) gRPC_windows_prebuilt Build information for each version Cpp-gRPC-Visual-Studio-Examples Source of the Visual Studio examples

docs.title: Who should use this project?
docs.text:
This project is a good fit if you:

  • Want to start with gRPC on Windows quickly, without building it from source.
  • Need the same gRPC binaries for every developer and every CI agent of a team.
  • Use Visual Studio solutions (.sln) or CMake with find_package.
  • Must stay on C++11 or an older Visual Studio version (see Version Compatibility).

docs.title: Which gRPC versions are available?
docs.text:
• Latest stable build: v1.85.3
  • Last build requiring only C++11: v1.46.7

All available versions, from v1.20.0 up to the latest, are in the release table.

docs.title: What compilers are supported?
docs.text:
The following Microsoft Visual C++ compiler toolsets are supported:

Visual Studio Toolset gRPC versions Visual Studio 2026 MSVC 145 v1.85.0 and later Visual Studio 2022 MSVC 143 all current releases Visual Studio 2019 MSVC 142 up to v1.84.x Visual Studio 2017 MSVC 141 up to v1.45.1, and v1.46.7 Visual Studio 2015 MSVC 140 up to v1.45.x

Each toolset is available for 32-bit (x86) and 64-bit (x64). The release table shows the exact toolsets of each version.

docs.title: What build configurations are available?
docs.text:
Each library archive contains three build configurations:

  • Debug - No optimization, full debug symbols. Use it for development.
  • RelWithDebInfo - Optimized, with debug symbols. Use it for production builds that you must debug.
  • Release - Optimized, without debug symbols.

docs.title: How do I download the prebuilt libraries?
docs.text:
You have two options:

  1. Direct from GitHub Releases: Navigate to the releases page and select your desired gRPC version.

  2. Release Version Table: Check the available versions in the release version table.

docs.title: What files should I download?
docs.text:
For each gRPC version, you need to download:

  1. Library archives (e.g., MSVC143_64.zip, MSVC142_32.zip) - Contains precompiled .lib files and header directories
  2. Examples archive (Examples.zip) - Contains Visual Studio project files for all supported compiler versions

docs.title: How do I organize the downloaded files?
docs.text:
Extract all archives into a single project directory with the following structure:

your-project/
├─ vs2015/                    # Visual Studio 2015 projects (from Examples.zip)
├─ vs2017/                    # Visual Studio 2017 projects (from Examples.zip)
├─ vs2019/                    # Visual Studio 2019 projects (from Examples.zip)
├─ vs2022/                    # Visual Studio 2022 projects (from Examples.zip)
├─ MSVC140_32/                # VS2015 32-bit headers/libs
├─ MSVC140_64/                # VS2015 64-bit headers/libs
├─ MSVC141_32/                # VS2017 32-bit headers/libs
├─ MSVC141_64/                # VS2017 64-bit headers/libs
├─ MSVC142_32/                # VS2019 32-bit headers/libs
├─ MSVC142_64/                # VS2019 64-bit headers/libs
├─ MSVC143_32/                # VS2022 32-bit headers/libs
├─ MSVC143_64/                # VS2022 64-bit headers/libs
├─ MSVC145_32/                # VS2026 32-bit headers/libs
└─ MSVC145_64/                # VS2026 64-bit headers/libs

docs.title: Do I need to install gRPC from source?
docs.text:
No! The prebuilt libraries include all necessary components:

  • Precompiled .lib files for linking
  • Required header files (grpc/, protobuf/ directories)
  • Visual Studio project examples (pre-configured and debuggable)

docs.title: How do I build the examples in Visual Studio?
docs.text:
1. Open the appropriate solution file:

    • vs2015/HelloWorld.sln for Visual Studio 2015
    • vs2017/HelloWorld.sln for Visual Studio 2017
    • vs2019/HelloWorld.sln for Visual Studio 2019
    • vs2022/HelloWorld.sln for Visual Studio 2022

  2. Ensure the correct compiler toolset is selected in Visual Studio options

  3. Build the solution:

    • Menu: Build → Build Solution
    • Shortcut: Ctrl+Shift+B

  4. The output will be organized as:

    _out_/
└─ <architecture>/          # x64 or x86
   └─ <build configuration>/ # Debug, Release, or RelWithDebInfo
      └─ <example binaries>  # executables and resources

docs.title: What examples are available?
docs.text:
Starting from gRPC v1.43.0, the following examples are included:

Example Description HelloWorld Basic client/server communication Client Callback / Server Callback Asynchronous callback patterns Async Client/Server Modern async implementations Compression gRPC compression support Load Balancing Client-side load balancing Meta Metadata handling examples KeyValueStore Key-value store service Route Guide Complex routing scenarios

docs.title: How do I debug the examples?
docs.text:
The Debug and RelWithDebInfo configurations include symbol files (.pdb) for debugging. Simply:

  1. Set breakpoints in your code
  2. Run the example with F5 or use the Debug toolbar
  3. Inspect variables, call stacks, and execution flow

docs.title: "Cannot find module 'grpc'" error
docs.text:
Cause: Visual Studio cannot locate the gRPC header files.

Solution:

  1. Verify that the grpc/ directory exists in your project root
  2. Check that the include paths in your .vcxproj file point to the correct locations
  3. Ensure you downloaded both library archives and examples archive

docs.title: "MSB8028: No target specified" error
docs.text:
Cause: The solution file was opened with an incompatible Visual Studio version.

Solution:

  1. Close Visual Studio
  2. Open the solution with the matching Visual Studio version (e.g., vs2019/*.sln with VS 2019)
  3. Rebuild the solution

docs.title: "LNK1181: cannot open input file" error
docs.text:
Cause: The precompiled library files are missing or in the wrong location.

Solution:

  1. Verify that all required .lib files exist in their respective architecture folders
  2. Check that the library path is correctly specified in the project properties
  3. Ensure you downloaded archives for both 32-bit and 64-bit if needed

docs.title: "Configuration 'Release' is not available" error
docs.text:
Cause: Attempting to build with a configuration that doesn't exist.

Solution: Use one of the three supported configurations: Debug, RelWithDebInfo, or Release.

docs.title: Where can I find more help?
docs.text:
• Check the setup instructions for detailed installation steps
  • Create a GitHub issue for specific problems

docs.title: Which C++ standard do I need?
docs.text:
gRPC version Minimum C++ standard v1.47.0 and later C++14 (newer gRPC versions can require a newer standard, see the gRPC release notes) v1.46.7 and older C++11

gRPC C++ v1.47.0 is the first release that requires C++14. If you cannot upgrade to C++14, use v1.46.7, the last release that requires only C++11.

docs.title: What changed in v1.78.1?
docs.text:
Starting with gRPC v1.78.1, the deployment layout for CMake files changed:

  • The cmake directory was moved from the project root to the lib directory
  • This change simplifies integration using find_package

docs.title: Do older Visual Studio versions still work?
docs.text:
Yes, but only with older gRPC versions:

  • Visual Studio 2019 (MSVC 142): up to gRPC v1.84.x
  • Visual Studio 2017 (MSVC 141): up to gRPC v1.45.1, and v1.46.7
  • Visual Studio 2015 (MSVC 140): up to gRPC v1.45.x

From gRPC v1.85.0, releases are built for Visual Studio 2026 (MSVC 145) and Visual Studio 2022 (MSVC 143). See What compilers are supported? for the full list.
